title: MFA fatigue
overview: An employee receives repeated, unexpected sign-in approval prompts. Inspect identity logs and decide when repeated denials deserve investigation.
prerequisites: Read the baseline and compare event fields. No external tools are required.

attack.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
attack.rationale: The behavior in this lesson corresponds to this technique; the fixture models a defensive observation.

hypothesis: Three distinct denied push prompts for one user within five minutes warrant investigation.
evidence: Confirm the user, method and outcome. Three distinct challenge IDs within five minutes link the alert to individual requests.
false_positive: Someone re-enrolling a phone can deny repeated prompts. An approved enrollment test is recorded with a change context.
tuning: Check user impact and enrollment history. Set thresholds from known login behavior and review any training-account exceptions.
response: Contact the user through a trusted channel. If a prompt was unexpectedly approved, revoke sessions and review subsequent sign-ins.
prevention: Require phishing-resistant MFA where possible. Enable number matching and authentication throttling for remaining push users.
validation: Baseline and noisy fixture produce no alerts. The positive fixture produces an alert with linked evidence.
limitations: The sample records prompt denials. Confirming account compromise requires independent sign-in and session evidence.

questions.prompt: What makes these prompt denials one alert?
options: Three distinct pushes for one user in five minutes
Three prompts anywhere in the tenant
questions.explanation: The rule groups by user and counts distinct challenge IDs within a five-minute window.

questions.prompt: What should you verify with the user?
options: Whether the account uses a long display name
Whether the prompts were expected or approved
questions.explanation: Unexpected prompts can indicate attempted access. Approval changes the response priority.
